strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse domains (DNA generation, Atari macro-actions, multi-agent RL) with strong empirical results: state-of-the-art on DNA generation (highest reward and log-likelihood), competitive/superior performance on 36/56 Atari games, substantial improvements in multi-agent football scenarios

Principled technical approach combining Policy Mirror Descent with discrete diffusion models for distributional matching; clean mathematical derivation of forward and reverse KL objectives with practical approximations

Excellent scalability analysis demonstrating the method scales effectively with increased computational resources (Figures 3-4), addressing the horizon-complexity trade-off central to combinatorial RL

Practical innovations including on-policy diffusion learning (Section 4.2) that aligns training and inference distributions, elegant temperature tuning via hard KL constraints (Appendix C.2), and inference-time efficiency techniques (top-p sampling, remasking)

Thorough experimental details and reproducibility: extensive appendices with hyperparameters, architectural specifications, implementation details for each domain, and comprehensive ablation studies on temperature tuning, on-policy training, and network architecture
weaknesses: Approximation quality and impact not rigorously analyzed: FKL loss relies on ELBO lower bound (Appendix B.1) whose tightness is not quantified; RKL uses biased importance sampling estimators (η̂_ELBO admits error term Γ) and crude single-step approximation that break theoretical guarantees, but approximation error is not empirically or theoretically bounded

Lack of convergence analysis: while PMD has known convergence guarantees (Lan 2023), the practical algorithm introduces multiple approximations (ELBO bounds, biased IS ratios, single-step approximations) and uses off-policy replay buffers, yet provides no convergence rate, sample complexity, or asymptotic analysis

Insufficient ablation of core design choices: on-policy diffusion learning (Section 4.2) shows only modest improvement (~5-10% in Fig. 9) without clear justification of added complexity; no systematic ablation comparing FKL vs RKL choices across domains; missing comparison with standard supervised diffusion training to isolate PMD contribution

Experimental claims overstated relative to evidence: 'state-of-the-art' claim not well-supported in Atari (Table 5 shows overlapping confidence intervals with R2D2/PPO; RL-D² underperforms on some games like Atlantis); 'superior sample efficiency' not convincingly demonstrated in Fig. 2; statistical significance testing lacking despite high variance across games

Limited baseline comparisons in specialized domains: Atari experiments missing recent structured action space methods; DNA limited to single-step setting with mostly guidance/distillation baselines; multi-agent comparisons limited to one autoregressive baseline, no independent learners or value decomposition methods

Critical implementation details missing or unclear: value function training procedure not specified in main text (TD(λ)? n-step?); replay buffer interaction with on-policy diffusion trajectories not explained (what is balance ratio?); temperature parameter λ mostly fixed without principled selection guidance; computational cost of on-policy data collection not fully accounted for

Limited theoretical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (PMD, distributional matching from prior work [Chan et al. 2022; Abdolmaleki et al. 2018], masked discrete diffusion). Main contribution is engineering/empirical rather than fundamental algorithmic or theoretical advance

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing scaling RL to large combinatorial action spaces with a novel distributional matching approach using Policy Mirror Descent
Comprehensive experimental validation across three diverse domains (DNA generation, Atari macro-actions, multi-agent RL) with state-of-the-art results in most cases
Thorough empirical analysis revealing the FKL vs. RKL trade-off with practical guidance for practitioners (sample efficiency vs. asymptotic performance)
Extensive ablation studies and detailed implementation details supporting reproducibility
Clear articulation of diffusion models' advantages over autoregressive policies through non-causal generation, with demonstrated benefits in complex coordination tasks
Large-scale experiments (56 Atari environments, sophisticated statistical analysis with stratified bootstrap CIs)
weaknesses: Lacks theoretical justification: no convergence guarantees or formal analysis of why distributional matching to the PMD solution ensures effective policy improvement; the approximation error from FKL's ELBO lower bound is unanalyzed

Fairness of baseline comparisons: DQN-Macro and IMPALA-Macro are simple adaptations designed to highlight diffusion's expressiveness advantage; comparison with more sophisticated combinatorial RL methods is limited; in MARL, MAT achieves comparable performance (e.g., 91.3% vs 99.4% on 11vs11) despite lacking non-causal design

Temperature hyperparameter tuning complexity inadequately emphasized in main paper: FKL exhibits catastrophic collapse with poor settings (Fig. 13), requires careful scheduling (linear decay 1.0→0.1), and lacks principled justification despite being critical to performance

Empirical validation is mixed: MinAtar shows improvement in only 2/5 tasks with underperformance on some (RL-D² 52.38 vs DQN-Macro 43.05 on Asterix); Atari scalability claims overstate results—performance degrades with fixed compute for macro-action length >4, with improvements only when proportionally increasing model capacity
On-Policy Diffusion Learning (Section 4.2) lacks clear motivation and ablation shows modest improvement (~5%); distinction between diffusion-process on-policy vs. overall RL framework is confusing

Insufficient guidance on when practitioners should prefer RL-D² over simpler alternatives; the practical advantage over MAT with permutations appears incremental, questioning whether the added complexity of diffusion policies and temperature tuning is justified

Potential confounds in Atari experiments: performance gains could stem from architectural choices (Transformers, residual networks) rather than the core diffusion policy contribution; architecture ablation (Fig. 16) is orthogonal to method validation
Some statistical results show overlapping confidence intervals with baselines (Fig. 9, Table 2), and failure mode analysis is absent

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse domains (DNA generation, Atari macro-actions, multi-agent RL) with extensive ablations and empirical analysis
Well-motivated problem addressing combinatorial action spaces and thorough technical presentation with detailed derivations and implementation details
Practical insights about FKL vs RKL trade-offs (sample efficiency vs stability) and useful techniques (on-policy diffusion learning, remasking, top-p sampling)
Clear computational efficiency gains in some settings (e.g., 66.4GB to 10.6GB memory reduction vs DRAKES on DNA task)
Generally solid technical execution with proper statistical analysis using stratified bootstrap confidence intervals
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—core contribution is straightforward combination of existing techniques (PMD + discrete diffusion); no novel algorithmic insight or theoretical understanding beyond engineering integration

Critical unfair comparisons in Atari: RL-D² uses Transformers while baselines use standard architectures; ablation (Fig. 16) shows transformers significantly outperform MLPs, undermining claims about diffusion superiority and confounding results
Mixed empirical results undermine claims of superiority: only 2/5 improvements on MinAtar, 36/56 on Atari with many improvements within confidence intervals or statistically marginal

High method complexity and brittleness: FKL requires domain-specific temperature/KL constraint tuning (Appendix E.3 shows collapse with wrong temperature); different schedules needed per domain with no principled selection procedure

Complete absence of theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, approximation error analysis, or theoretical explanation for empirical FKL vs RKL differences—purely empirical treatment of fundamental questions

Weak baseline implementations: DQN-Macro and IMPALA-Macro use non-standard designs; no comparison to established hierarchical RL methods; baselines in Google Football appear undertuned (MAPPO underperforms expectations)

No clear guidance on applicability or when practitioners should use RL-D² over alternatives; critical component ablations missing (PMD alone, diffusion with standard RL, diffusion vs other expressive policies)
Mentioned black-box solvers (ES, CEM) in introduction but never experimentally compared despite being relevant baselines for combinatorial optimization

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations of existing methods (exponential scaling, causal constraints in autoregressive models) with a principled solution via PMD-based distributional matching

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse domains (DNA, Atari macro-actions, multi-agent RL) with rigorous statistical analysis (50k bootstrap iterations), extensive ablations, and detailed implementation details enabling reproducibility
Strong empirical results: achieves SOTA on DNA generation, outperforms on 36/56 Atari tasks (mean 31.33 vs 18.01), and best performance on complex multi-agent coordination tasks (5v5, 11v11 football)

Practical contributions including clear FKL vs RKL trade-off guidance (Section 5.4), temperature tuning via KL constraints, efficient sampling techniques, and demonstration of scalability to macro-action length 16 where baselines fail
Thorough presentation with honest discussion of limitations, detailed appendices with proofs and implementation details, and clear motivation for design choices
weaknesses: Limited theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees or sample complexity bounds; loose ELBO bound used in FKL and its implications for policy improvement not discussed; on-policy diffusion learning (Section 4.2) lacks theoretical justification

Temperature tuning brittleness: FKL explicitly prone to collapse if temperature not properly tuned (Fig. 13); different KL schedules required across domains (1.0→0.1 decay for Atari vs fixed 0.1 for Football); auto-tuning adds another hyperparameter (ε) requiring domain-specific selection, limiting practical applicability

Baseline comparison concerns: DQN-Macro and IMPALA-Macro are somewhat strawman approaches; more meaningful comparisons (MAT, MAPPO) show smaller margins; missing comparisons with other recent diffusion RL methods; 20/56 Atari tasks show worse performance than baselines

Approximations in policy objectives not fully analyzed: FKL reweighting may introduce bias with unquantified error; RKL uses single-step ratio instead of full trajectory ratio, a significant approximation with unknown impact; no ablation on these choices

Limited novelty: PMD, discrete diffusion models, and their combination are relatively incremental; main contribution is deriving FKL/RKL objectives, which is solid but not a fundamental algorithmic advance

Generalization unclear: all experiments involve discrete sequences or joint actions; applicability to other combinatorial problems (graphs, permutations, optimization) not demonstrated; limited analysis of which diffusion-specific properties (non-causality, flexibility) actually matter

Incomplete computational cost analysis: DNA memory reduction claimed but only 2.8x wall-clock speedup vs DRAKES; Atari wall-clock time comparison against baselines not provided; no clear guidance on when computational overhead is justified

Design choices lack motivation: on-policy diffusion learning (sampling from p_θ rather than q for training) benefits unclear; diffusion timestep selection (200 for DNA, 32+ for Atari) not justified; architecture ablation doesn't isolate diffusion-specific benefits from Transformer capacity
